title: Crawler Seen Pages
story: A small search startup crawls the web and must not fetch the same page twice. Keeping every URL it has seen in memory is too much: at about 100 bytes a URL, a billion URLs is 100 GB. A Bloom filter answers "have I seen this URL?" with about 10 bits per URL, so 1.25 GB for the same billion. The catch: it can say "maybe seen" for a URL it never saw (the crawler then skips a page it should have fetched), but it never says "not seen" for a URL that was added.

The same structure sits in front of disk lookups in key-value stores, to skip reading files that cannot hold a key, and in front of caches, to drop requests for keys that do not exist. See Design a Web Crawler and Design a Key-Value Store.
task: Write a class SeenFilter with a bit array of m bits, all 0 at the start, and k hash positions per URL:
• add(url): set the bits at all k positions of url to 1.
• mightContain(url): return true if all k positions of url are 1, otherwise false.
• bitsSet(): return how many of the m bits are 1.
The positions come from two fixed hashes of the URL, spelled out here so every solution picks the same bits. For each character from left to right, with c its character code:
Position i, for i from 0 to k − 1, is (h1 + i × h2) mod m. Two positions of one URL may be the same bit.
constraints: Each URL has 1 to 100 printable ASCII characters (codes 33 to 126)

examples.explanation: For "cats.io", h1 = 750,493,409 and h2 = 956,570,721, so the positions are 750,493,409 mod 16 = 1, then 2, then 3. "dogs.io" sets 9, 8, 7 and "owls.io" sets 11, 5, 15: 9 bits in all. "dogs.io" was added, so it is found. "yaks.io" needs bits 2, 15 and 12; bit 12 is 0, so it was certainly never added. "bats.io" needs bits 7, 1 and 11, which other URLs happened to set: a false positive. The filter says "maybe" for a URL it never saw.

hints: A plain set stores the URLs themselves. What could you store instead if you were allowed to be wrong in one direction only?
Store only bits. Adding a URL turns on a few bits chosen by hashing it. If any of those bits is still off later, the URL was never added; if all are on, it probably was.
Compute h1 and h2 once per URL, then get the k positions from (h1 + i × h2) mod m. Take each step of the hash modulo its prime, so the numbers stay small enough for exact JavaScript arithmetic.
Use an array of m booleans or 0/1 values, and keep a counter that goes up only when a bit changes from 0 to 1, so bitsSet is O(1). Do not count a bit twice when two positions coincide.
bruteForce: A hash set of every URL is exact, but it stores the URLs: about 100 GB for a billion of them, which does not fit in one machine's memory, so every check becomes a network or disk lookup.
The Bloom filter trades exactness for size. With about 10 bits per URL and 7 hash positions, the false positive rate is roughly (1 − e−0.7)7 ≈ 0.8%, for 1.25 GB instead of 100 GB.

walkthrough: The filter is an array of bits. Adding sets k bits picked by hashing; checking reads the same k bits. Getting k positions from two hashes, h1 + i × h2, is a standard trick that avoids computing k separate hash functions.
• "yaks.io" needs 2, 15, 12. Bit 12 is off: definitely not seen.
• "bats.io" needs 7, 1, 11, all on: "maybe seen", though it never was.

Why there are no false negatives: adding only ever turns bits on, so the bits of an added URL stay on. That is also why you cannot delete from a plain Bloom filter: turning a bit off could erase another URL. Size it up front: with n URLs and m bits, the best k is about (m / n) × 0.69, and the filter gets worse as it fills, as the crowded test shows.
solution.timeWhy: Each call hashes the URL once (L characters) and touches k bits.
solution.spaceWhy: The bit array; the URLs themselves are never stored.
solution.takeaway: A Bloom filter answers "definitely not" or "maybe" for set membership in a few bits per item. Use it in front of something expensive (a disk read, a fetch, a database lookup) where an occasional unnecessary "maybe" is cheap and a wrong "no" is not allowed.
